title: Cap. X Arg. IV: open advocates grant the consequence and find no absurdity — Lessius; but Paul refers both reprobation and election to God's antecedent will of mercy and non-mercy by good pleasure
pass_a_gloss: They who more openly plead this cause acknowledge the force of the consequence, but by no means judge it absurd to embrace (as they speak) that election and reprobation depend from the acts of human choice. So philosophizes the Jesuit Lessius. But because the Apostle clearly and perspicuously referred both reprobation and election unto the antecedent will of God, having mercy and not having mercy according to his good pleasure, others are compelled to answer otherwise.
pass_b_english: Those who plead this cause more openly grant the force of the consequence, yet find no absurdity in holding — as they speak — that election and reprobation depend on acts of human choice. So the Jesuit Lessius philosophizes. But because the Apostle clearly and plainly referred both reprobation and election to God's antecedent will — having mercy and not having mercy according to his good pleasure — others are forced to answer otherwise.
source_text: Qui apertius hanc causam agunt, agnoscunt vim consequentiae, sed minime absurdum arbitrantur, complecti (ut illi loquuntur) electionem et reprobationem ex humani arbitrii actibus dependere. Sic philosophatur Lessius Jesuita. Sed quia Apostolus tam reprobationem quam electionem clare et perspicue retulit ad antecedentem Dei voluntatem, miserentis et non miserentis pro suo beneplacito, alii coguntur aliter respondere.
